title: Ready to run your mini-PD
goal: Turn your one page into a short session you'll actually deliver — and handle pushback calmly.

blocks.title: From page to staffroom
blocks.body:
You've got your one-pager from the last lesson. Now the real step: getting it in front of colleagues.

It doesn't need a projector, a slide deck, or an hour. Fifteen minutes in a free period, four or five colleagues, and your page on the table is plenty. Let's get it ready.

blocks.title: The whole recipe: demo, rule, question
blocks.body:
A mini-PD that lands is honestly just three moves:

1. One live demo — make one real thing in front of them (a worksheet, a parent note). Seeing it beats hearing about it.
2. One shared rule — agree on a single habit together, like "keep student details out of the tool." One rule people remember beats ten they forget.
3. One question invited — end by asking "where would this actually save you time?" You're starting a conversation, not giving a lecture.

Demo, rule, question. That's the session.
blocks.goDeeper: Keep your one-pager as the handout. The demo shows it's real, the rule makes it safe, the question makes it theirs — and the page means nobody has to remember it all.

blocks.question: Mid-session, the staffroom skeptic folds their arms: "I don't have time to learn another new tool." What's your best move?

options.text: Explain all the features so they see how powerful it is.
Agree the time worry is fair, then show one two-minute thing that saves them time this week — and let the result speak.
Tell them the school expects everyone to try it.

blocks.explanation: You met the objection with respect, not a sales pitch. A skeptic is won by a small, real time-saving — shown, not argued — never by pressure or a feature dump. Their caution is reasonable; honour it.

blocks.question: When, and with which colleagues, will you run your first fifteen-minute session? Name it — that's how it actually happens.
